line: Sat sri akal. Harjit Singh. I come here for the chai, mostly. You're new?
choice1: Yes, I just moved in. I'm {playerName}.

line: Welcome, welcome. The chai is free if you don't ask who made it. Where are you living?
choice1: On Grand, near the bus stop.
choice3: I'll get some chai. See you.

line: Good, a short drive. I used to drive long ones. Thirty-one years in a truck, coast to coast.
Everywhere. Interstate 80, mostly. Best pie in Nebraska, around mile marker 177. Worst coffee in Wyoming. _laughs_ Every stop in Wyoming. I think it's a state law.
choice2: What did you do all day on the road?
choice3: I'll let you drink your chai.

line: Some days. My wife says I still recite the mile markers in my sleep. Now I drive to the gurdwara, the park, and here. Very short routes.
choice1: What do you do at the gurdwara?

line: Radio, and calls home from the pay phones, back then. Punjabi radio once I got near Fresno. Then nothing for six hundred miles.
choice1: Where did you start out from?

line: A village near Ludhiana. When I came, I'd never driven anything bigger than a tractor. The man who trained me in Stockton said, it's a tractor that doesn't stop. He was right.
Every few years, for weddings. The village has a paved road now, all the way in. My cousins drive it like it's Interstate 80. I hold the door handle.
On Sundays I cook in the langar, the free kitchen. Three hundred people some weeks. Anybody can eat.
choice3: Sounds like hard work. See you.

line: Anybody. Cover your head, take off your shoes, sit on the floor. Last month two firefighters came in from the station on Ninth. The next week they came back with their wives.
Come one Sunday. I'll put you on rotis. Everybody's first rotis are ugly. Mine were ugly for a year.
Sat sri akal. Don't mind the phone, it's cricket. Harjit Singh. You walk here?
I do two laps and then I sit, and the cricket does the rest. My doctor only counts the laps.
India and Australia, in Melbourne. It's three in the morning there. My grandson says, Nanaji, watch baseball, it's on right now.
Every game. He's a catcher, Jaspreet. I still don't understand why the man who catches is the most tired.
At his high school, Thursdays. I sit at the top of the bleachers with a thermos. The other grandfathers think it's beer. It's chai. Nobody believes me.
Good morning! Sit. I'm early, the chai isn't. Somebody forgot to put the water on.
No, early morning. My grandson had a game last night. Jaspreet. He plays baseball, catcher.
Lost by one. He says it was the umpire. I said, in cricket we say the same thing. He said, Nanaji, it's not the same.
It's the same. A man in a hat decides your whole day. $ He was born in Fresno. He doesn't play cricket. But he lets me explain it, which is kind of him.
choice1: Do you mind that he doesn't play?

line: No. He's good at baseball. When I came, I wanted my son to be good at things here. Now his son is. Ah, the water's boiling.
Good morning! Sit, sit. Today I put the water on myself, so the chai is already coming.
Only the big pot. _points at the notice board_ Somebody wrote: chai for thirty, Thursday, library. Underlined two times. I know who.
Meena. She runs this place now. She says, Harjit-ji, you have the biggest pot. She's right, I do. So on Thursday I drive my pot to the library.
choice1: What do you think of her?
choice3: I'll let you get the chai.

line: I like her. She talks to everybody like they're already coming. $ The librarian came to langar on Sunday, because Meena asked her. She made ugly rotis. Very good ugly rotis.
choice1: That sounds like a good Sunday.

line: Good morning! You're early, the hall is quiet. Enjoy it. It lasts until nine.
At nine the board comes. Thursday is board day. Big table, small biscuits.
choice3: I'll stay out of their way.

line: Mr. Deshpande runs it. Runs the whole association, twenty-five years. He reads the minutes out loud, every number. Last meeting, forty minutes on the roof.
choice1: What do you think of him?
choice3: I'll let you enjoy the quiet.

line: Good man. Stubborn like a Wyoming wind. He says the hall should look after its own and not wait for the city. $ [warm] Me, I drive to the gurdwara, I drive here, I drive to the park. I like all the roads open.
choice1: All the roads open. I like that.

line: Hello, hello. _turns the phone so you can see_ Cricket, from Melbourne. Sit if you like.
Two hundred and forty for six. That's good, believe me. It's three in the morning there, so I'm watching people who should be asleep.
choice1: How long does a game last?
choice2: I'll take your word for it.

line: This kind, five days. My grandson says baseball is long. I tell him, you don't know long.
In the village, with a plank and a tennis ball wrapped in tape. Then thirty-one years on the road, no cricket. Radio when I could get it, near the coast.
choice1: And now it's on your phone.

line: Now it's on my phone, in a park, in America, propped on a water bottle. _laughs_ If you told the boy with the plank, he'd say you were lying.
Ah, {playerName}. Sit with me a minute? My chai is hot and my stories are long.
You remember I told you about the pie in Nebraska? I never told you about the rest of that stop.
Twenty years on the road, I was the only turban at most truck stops. Most people were fine. They asked about the miles, the weather.
Some days, not fine. After 2001 especially. A man in Rawlins wouldn't serve me coffee. $ [warm] Which, in Wyoming, I should have thanked him for.
choice1: What did you do on those days?

line: I drove to the next stop. And I called my wife and told her about the pie, not the coffee. You're the first person I've told the coffee part to in a long time.
Because you listen and don't make a face. And because Jaspreet will drive someday, and I want to know how to tell him. Okay. Enough. Drink your chai.
Ah, hello. Excuse me, I've been on the phone with my nephew all morning.
choice2: I'll let you call him back.

line: He drives a truck now, like me. Last week at a weigh station they checked his papers twice.
They didn't say. Then they asked about his turban. Was it religious, did he have to wear it.
choice3: I'm sorry. I'll let you go.

line: He said, I'm from Fresno, sir. He was born there. I was in the waiting room. After an hour they let him go.
He's angry, which is better than scared. He asked me what I did, in my time. I told him I drove to the next stop. He didn't like that answer.
choice1: Maybe he'll find a different one.

line: Ah, hello! My wife made me watch the news twice last night.
The president said something kind about Sikhs. Our name, on the television, said correctly.
She watched it twice and then said, now he has to do something. Thirty-nine years married. She's always the second sentence.
She is. Me, I'm happy with kind words, I'm an old man. But Jaspreet was watching too. He turned the volume up. He never turns up the news.
He said, Nanaji, they said it right. The name. That's all. Then he went back to his phone.
Every time I come for chai, you're here! Good.
Mr. Deshpande likes you, you know. He doesn't say so.
He moves his chair to make room. That's how he says so. For me it took two years.
I wasn't here much. The road. And the gurdwara is my place on Sundays. This hall is everybody, Gujaratis, Tamils, Punjabis, all arguing about the roof. I like that too.
choice1: Do you feel at home here?

line: Home is my wife's kitchen. Here is chai and arguing. The gurdwara is the langar. Three places, all short routes. Enough for one old man.
Every time I come for chai, you're here! Good.
Meena has your name on her list, you know. She doesn't hide it.
The list of people who say yes. She finds you a job before you know you said it. Me, she put on chai for the library nights. Thirty cups. I said yes before she finished.
choice1: Do you feel at home here?
choice3: I'll watch out for her list.

line: Ah! Jaspreet says he saw you at the ball field. With the other parents.
Catchers see everything. Good, good. Then you can explain to me what is a balk.
choice1: Nobody knows what a balk is.

line: That's what the umpire said! I asked him. He said, sir, it's complicated. Like the coffee in Wyoming.
choice1: Do you go to all his games?

line: All of them. At first I sat at the top with the other Punjabi grandfathers. Now the pitcher's father saves me a spot by the fence. He brings sunflower seeds, I bring chai. We don't talk much.
Careful, careful, walk around. _points at the floor by the door_ The rangoli. Somebody's grandmother made it at six this morning, and today I am the guard.
choice3: I'll go the long way. See you.

line: Mrs. Joshi, from the language school. Orange, yellow, green, one lamp. At four o'clock a boy ran straight through it. She didn't say a word. She started again from the corner.

On the road you learn the same thing. The load shifts, you pull over, you strap it again. You don't argue with the load. $ Now go in, there's chai. And the Tuesday column on the kitchen sheet is still empty. I'm only saying.
choice1: Put me down for a Tuesday.

line: Harjit nods and goes back to his phone.
Ah, it's nothing. Thirty-one years on the road, you learn everybody has a bad day. Sit, the chai is fresh.
Last over. If I look away now, they lose. It's my fault every time.
